scope.summary: This Indian Standard prescribes the methods for grading and visual classification of muscovite mica blocks, thins, and films based on their size, thickness, and visual quality traits to govern commercial grading, electrical component sorting, and industrial trade.

certification_and_marking.standard_type: Material Grading & Visual Classification Standard (Electrotechnical Department / Mica)
certification_and_marking.certification_status: Voluntary Quality Grading Standard. Muscovite mica blocks, thins, and films are visually graded and sorted in processing yards prior to electrical fabrication or export based on these criteria.

requirements.detail: Quality classification is highly subjective, carried out manually by individual workers, and heavily influenced by circumstantial factors such as lighting conditions and the inspector's mood. Thus, the standard can give at best an approximate idea of a particular quality's relative position.
Visual classification guidelines specified in this standard may or may not have any direct bearings on the actual functional end use of the mica.

Establishes unified symbols to evaluate permissible defect levels: x = Not Permissible, v = Very Slight, p = Permissible, s = Slight, l = Limited Extent, h = Heavy, and Blank Indication = Not Applicable.
Classifies the highest-tier commercial block size using the designation '250 / (SPECIAL)'.
Establishes numerical size and thickness grading benchmarks: No. 1 (160 - 10), No. 2 (100), 63, No. 3 (40), No. 4 (5), 5 V, and No. 5 (0.6) to classify structural area and thickness boundaries.

plain_language_summary.summary: IS : 1175 - 1981 (First Revision) is the primary national Indian Standard specification prescribing methods for the grading and visual classification of Muscovite Mica blocks, thins, and films. Maintained under the Mica Sectional Committee (ETDC 9) and reaffirmed up to 2016, the code unifies size designations (ranging from No. 5 up to the special '250 / (SPECIAL)' grade) and establishes a standard defect permissibility coding system (using symbols like 'x' for not permissible and 'p' for permissible). Due to the natural complexity of mica minerals, the standard acknowledges that quality sorting remains highly subjective—conducted manually by individual workers and influenced by lighting and human factors—offering an approximate, industry-accepted framework for visual commercial grading.
